## What the log shows

First, a flag: **every line in `logs/app.log` is timestamped `2026-07-04`, 02:00–02:31 UTC.** Today is 2026-08-19, so this file is about six weeks old — it is not last night's outage. Either the log rotated and this is a stale copy, or the incident you're thinking of is in a different file. Everything below describes the July 4 event that *is* in this file.

### Timeline (all times UTC, 2026-07-04)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 02:00:00 – 02:14:03 | Healthy. 173 × `200` responses, cache hit ratio 0.90–0.98, cron ticks fine. |
| **02:14:07.113** | `ERROR [api] redis connection lost: connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.0.12:6379` |
| 02:14:07.114 | App fails open: `cache layer degraded — falling back to direct store reads` |
| 02:14:08 | First `cache miss storm` |
| 02:14:10 | First `TimeoutError: request timed out after 5000ms (store overloaded)` — 3s after Redis died |
| 02:15:26 | First reconnect attempt (`attempt 0`), then 12 more, all refused |
| 02:29:12 | Request queue crosses its limit: `depth 502 (max 500)` |
| 02:31:44 | `ERROR [worker-2] JavaScript heap out of memory (request backlog)` |
| 02:31:45 | `FATAL [supervisor] worker-2 exited with code 134, restarting` |
| **02:31:52** | `FATAL [supervisor] api unresponsive, killing process group — service down` |

### What actually happened

Redis at `10.0.0.12:6379` went away and never came back. `ECONNREFUSED` (not a timeout) means the port was actively refusing connections — the Redis process was down or the port was closed, not a network partition or a slow server. All 13 reconnect attempts over the next 16 minutes got the same refusal.

The outage is a **cache-stampede cascade**, and the app's own fallback is what killed it. On losing Redis it fell back to direct store reads instead of shedding load. Every request that would have been a 90–98% cache hit became a backing-store query, the store saturated within seconds, and 5-second timeouts started. Because timed-out requests were retained rather than dropped, the queue grew monotonically — +3 per sample, 52 at 02:14:12 up to 568 at 02:31:24 — until worker-2 exhausted the V8 heap holding the backlog. Exit code 134 is SIGABRT, the standard signature of a Node OOM abort. Seven seconds after that, the supervisor gave up on `api` and killed the process group.

Note the traffic blackout: **the last successful response is at 02:14:03**, one line before the Redis error. There are zero `200`s in the remaining 17m49s. This wasn't gradual degradation with partial availability — the service was effectively down from the moment the cache disappeared, and it took 17 minutes for the supervisor to formally declare it.

### Two things worth fixing

**The retry cadence has no backoff and no jitter.** The gaps between reconnect attempts are 80.3, 79.5, 80.3, 80.3, 79.5… — flat 80 seconds. Combined with the 79-second delay before the *first* attempt, if Redis had recovered at 02:16:00 the app wouldn't have noticed until 02:17:26. For a dependency this critical you want sub-second initial retries ramping up, not a fixed 80s poll.

**Only `[api]` logs reconnect attempts.** `worker-1`, `worker-2`, and `scheduler` all report cache misses and timeouts but never a single reconnect. Either they share the api's client, or they silently stopped trying to recover — worth checking which.

The real remediation is the fallback policy: on cache loss, the service needs a circuit breaker and load shedding (bounded queue that rejects with 503 when full, request coalescing on hot keys) rather than passing full traffic to the backing store. The queue's `max 500` was logged as a warning threshold but never actually enforced — depth sailed past it to 568 with no backpressure.

### Caveats

The repo contains only `package.json` and this log — no `src/`, so I couldn't verify the retry config or fallback logic against the code; the `ioredis ^5.4.1` dependency is consistent with what the log shows. The log also starts abruptly at exactly 02:00:00.000 with no preceding context, so I can't tell you whether a deploy, config push, or Redis maintenance window triggered the failure — nothing in the file references one. Redis's own logs from 02:13–02:14 would settle that.

One oddity: response times in the healthy period cycle 12→145ms and reset, repeatedly, across all four components in lockstep. That's not organic traffic shape, so I wouldn't read anything into pre-incident latency.
